plate_findings.evidence: Radiographs demonstrate multiple calcified intra-articular osteochondral bodies
erosive changes and remodeling of the femoral head–neck junction

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left panel shows a hip radiograph with multiple calcified intra-articular loose bodies and erosive changes at the femoral head–neck junction, consistent with primary synovial chondromatosis. The caption explicitly attributes the imaging features to synovial chondromatosis of the hip. B: Right panel shows a hip radiograph with numerous ring-and-arc calcified loose bodies in the joint space and associated bone changes, consistent with primary synovial chondromatosis. The caption explicitly attributes the imaging features to synovial chondromatosis of the hip.

panels.figure_caption: Imaging features of primary synovial chondromatosis of the hip. Radiographs demonstrate multiple calcified intra-articular osteochondral bodies associated with erosive changes and remodeling of the femoral head–neck junction.
in_text_mentions: Plain radiographs (X-rays) can show the characteristic multiple loose bodies, particularly after they have calcified or ossified (Figure 1). However, in the early stages of the disease, the cartilaginous nodules might not be calcified, with a normal image at X-rays [23]. Calcified nodules within the joint space will be visible on X-rays. These calcifications frequently exhibit a chondroid mineralization pattern that reflects the mineralization of cartilage tissue [24].

findings.label: Clustered chondrocytes with binucleation
findings.evidence: clustered chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix without significant cytological atypia

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology at 50× showing multiple cartilaginous nodules with peripheral ossification, classic microscopic presentation of synovial chondromatosis. B: H&E histology at 200× showing clustered chondrocytes in hyaline matrix without significant atypia, classic microscopic presentation of synovial chondromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: Zmerly et al. Synovial Chondromatosis: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence on Diagnosis, Differential Diagnosis, and Management.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2026. doi:10.3390/medicina62071388. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: (A,B). Histological section of synovial chondromatosi. On haematoxylin and eosin at 50× of magnification, multiple cartilaginous nodules variably cellular with peripheral ossification are observed (A); at 200× of magnification clustered chondrocytes in a hyaline matrix without significant cytological atypia are evident (B).
in_text_mentions: Microscopically, the nodules consist of lobules of hyaline cartilage with increased cellularity and clustered chondrocytes embedded in a chondroid matrix; mild cytological atypia, binucleated chondrocytes, and focal calcification or endochondral ossification may be observed without implying malignancy [9,24,29] (Figure 4). Residual synovial lining tissue often occurs around the cartilage fragments.

panels.rationale: Single-panel coronal MRI of a human patient. The caption explicitly links the massive lobulated chondroid lesion to synovial chondromatosis, with suspected malignant degeneration; the visible lobulated chondroid mass supports inclusion as a synovial chondromatosis MRI manifestation. Confidence is reduced because chondrosarcoma is also named and histology was needed for definitive evidence.
panels.attribution_text: Ng et al. Malignant Transformation of Synovial Chondromatosis: A Systematic Review.. The open orthopaedics journal 2017. doi:10.2174/1874325001711010517. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure (3).
panels.figure_caption: Synovial chondrosarcoma in the setting of synovial chondromatosis 43 year-old female presenting with a massive localized chondroid lesion suspected to have malignant degeneration of synovial chondromatosis based on imaging (MRI, A) and symptomatology. Histologic evidence of chondrosarcoma, however, was only detected after resection of essentially the entire lesion.
in_text_mentions: on this systematic review of reported cases, objective diagnostic findings for SChS include medullary bone invasion on imaging or histology and pathologic findings consistent with grade II or III chondrosarcoma [30, 33, 34] (Fig. 2). Concerning features include rapid clinical progression of pain, local recurrence within 12 mos after resection, soft tissue infiltration of tumor, and large size [34] (Fig. 3). Similar to the diagnostic and grading challenges of other chondroid malignancies, accurate assessment of SChS requires consideration of clinical, radiographic and histologic findings [32].

in_text_mentions: The evaluation of lesions in the glenoid fossa on MRI was described as follows: “positive”, when hypointense loose bodies and hyperintense joint fluid (with or without homogeneous mass) were detected on T2-weighted sequence; “suspicious”, when cartilaginous loose bodies are not ossified or calcified yet, but an abnormal large amount of synovial fluid was collected and detected on T2-weighted images with capsular expansion [9]; “negative”, when none of the aforementioned items were found [1, 7, 10, 11] (Figs 1–3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Lateral radiograph of the right knee from a human patient showing multiple calcified intra-articular loose bodies, a textbook presentation of synovial chondromatosis; yellow arrow marks the calcified bodies. B: Axial MRI of the knee showing lobulated cartilaginous synovial masses with multiple loose bodies, consistent with synovial chondromatosis in a human patient; yellow arrow indicates the lesion. C: Gross specimen of surgically excised pearly cartilaginous nodules from the knee, the classic gross appearance of synovial chondromatosis in a human patient. D: Histologic section showing lobules of metaplastic hyaline cartilage, the defining microscopic feature of synovial chondromatosis in a human patient; yellow arrows mark the cartilage lobules.

panels.rationale: Single axial MRI panel of the left wrist/distal radioulnar joint from a human patient. The caption explicitly states calcified nodules consistent with synovial osteochondromatosis, and the article title confirms synovial osteochondromatosis of the distal radioulnar joint. The in-text describes a mass with high proton-density signal and irregular peripheral/nodular enhancement, supporting rim/septal synovial enhancement and lobulated chondroid masses; calcified nodules correspond to MRI signal-void calcific foci. Presentation is atypical because the imaging features were considered consistent with malignancy (malignant fibrous histiocytoma/fibrosarcoma). No annotations, skin, ethnicity, or age are shown or stated.

in_text_mentions: ase of synovial chondromatosis extending to the cranial base. Panoramic radiographs taken upon the patient’s first visit revealed multiple calcified particles in the right TMJ area. CT and MRI were consecutively performed for accurate diagnosis. Radiological examinations revealed multiple nodules within the joint capsule of the right TMJ, extending to the middle cranial fossa. The shape of the mandibular condyle appeared to be smooth. The patient was provisionally diagnosed with pigmented villonodular synovitis and subsequently admitted for surgical treatment (Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a is a low-magnification H&E section of a paraffin-embedded loose body from synovial chondromatosis, showing lobules of chondroid metaplastic cartilage. in_text_mentions: ssible bleeding sources within the knee. The implant interfaces were carefully examined, and they were all found to be well fixed. An arthroscopic synovectomy was performed, leaving the implants in place. A pathological examination revealed chondroid metaplasia covered by fibrin-like material (Figure 5). Upon careful histopathological examination by our pathologist, the structures that were originally identified as rice bodies were in fact small loose bodies from SC. in_text_mentions: We choose a shoulder arthroscopy using a deltopectoral approach to remove the tumors nodules. More than 50 shiny and solid bodies, with an average size of 10–15 mm, were retrieved ( Fig. 2 ). There were also several bodies within the coracoid process and the conjoint tendon. The synovial tissue, bursas, and cartilages appeared intact. Upon removing the particles, we complete a partial synovectomy to avoid the relapse. Histology of loose bodies and synovium confirmed the diagnosis of PSC without any evidence of malignant transformation ( Fig. 3 ).

panels.rationale: Single lateral ankle radiograph from a case report of bilateral synovial chondromatosis. It is a real human-patient image showing multiple calcified intra-articular loose bodies posterior and anterior to the tibiotalar joint, the hallmark manifestation of synovial chondromatosis, with arrow and arrowhead annotations. Disease attribution is directly supported by the panel-specific caption and the disease-focused article title. Joint spaces are maintained and no other disease is identified, so the panel is included; a small posterior malleolus osteophyte and mild degenerative change are noted only as proposed findings since they are absent from the vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Lateral right ankle radiograph with evidence of calcified loose bodies (arrow) posterior to the talotibial joint. Small loose bodies are also seen anteriorly to the joint (arrow head).
in_text_mentions: The radiographs illustrated several calcific loose bodies projecting posterior to the tibiotalar joint with additional loose bodies anterior to the joint. The ankle mortise and subtalar joint spaces were well maintained. A small osteophyte was noted at the posterior malleolus (Figure 1). Mild degenerative joint disease of the tibiotalar joint was also noted.

in_text_mentions: Histopathology [Figure 6] revealed circumscribed lobulated nodules of osteocartilaginous tissue with the stroma consisting of cellular fibroblastic tissue. panels.rationale: Real patient histopathology image of excised left ankle joint tissue from a case report on arthroscopic treatment of synovial chondromatosis. Caption and in-text text explicitly describe multiple well-defined hyaline cartilage nodules with clustered benign chondrocytes (degenerative atypia), which directly match the configured disease synovial chondromatosis. Black ellipse and arrows annotate the nodule and chondrocytes. No other disease is involved; no third-party restriction.
panels.attribution_text: Kunzler et al. Arthroscopic Treatment of Synovial Chondromatosis in the Ankle Joint.. Cureus 2017. doi:10.7759/cureus.1983. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Left Ankle Joint Histology. Left ankle joint histology shows multiple well-defined nodules consisting of hyaline cartilage containing clusters of benign-appearing chondrocytes, some with degenerative atypia, consistent with synovial chondromatosis. One cluster is outlined by black ellipse. Black arrows highlight benign chondrocytes.
in_text_mentions: Following removal, the loose bodies were sent to surgical pathology. The cartilage showed proliferative activity with large pleomorphic nuclei, which tended to be arranged in small bunches. Furthermore, ossification was partially found in the loose body (Figure 6C).

panels.rationale: Single axial T1-weighted MRI of the hip from a case report of massive synovial osteochondromatosis of the hip. The arrow marks extra-articular loose bodies and the asterisk the femoral vessels/iliopsoas region; the caption, in-text description and disease-focused article title all attribute the lesion to synovial chondromatosis, with a recognized extra-articular herniation-sac extension rather than a purely intra-articular joint snowstorm. Real patient diagnostic MRI, clearly annotated, so it qualifies for the library.
panels.attribution_text: Kataoka et al. Complete Resection of a Massive Synovial Osteochondromatosis of the Hip Using an Anterior Approach: A Report of Two Cases.. Case reports in orthopedics 2017. doi:10.1155/2017/9806863. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 8.
panels.figure_caption: T1-weighted axial image of extra-articular loose bodies (arrow) adjacent to the iliopsoas muscle and the femoral vessels (asterisk).
in_text_mentions: Arthrography showed a honeycomb appearance around her left hip joint (Figure 7). Upon MR imaging, axial images of the left hip joint revealed intra-articular and extra-articular mass lesions, one of which was located adjacent to the femoral vessels (Figure 8). These examination findings suggested synovial osteochondromatosis forming a herniation sac. Based on the radiographic features, we considered that arthroscopic resection concomitant with an open anterior approach was suitable for complete resection.

panels.rationale: Single frontal pelvic radiograph of a human patient. The caption and article title attribute the intra-articular calcified loose bodies to early synovial osteochondromatosis (the configured target disease), satisfying disease attribution via a disease-focused title plus a specific captioned manifestation. The yellow circle marks the coexisting avascular necrosis of the right femoral head, but the panel still visibly shows the target-disease finding (few calcified loose bodies), so it is included. Early-stage disease with only a few bodies is a recognized less-common presentation rather than the classic extensive snowstorm pattern, hence variant typicality; stage is early. Age is adult from the in-text 40-year-old female. No skin, ethnicity, or other applicable fields are assessable. [raw subtype: early]

panels.figure_caption: Frontal radiograph of pelvis including both proximal femurs. Avascular necrosis of right femoral head with reduced head volume and widened acetabulum. Early development of synovial osteochondromatosis was also evident showing few calcified loose bodies. The yellow circle encompasses the AVN of the right femoral head with reduced head volume and widened acetabulum. Early development of synovial osteochondromatosis was also evident, showing a few calcified loose bodies. AVN: Avascular necrosis
in_text_mentions: A 40-year-old female presented to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of right hip pain and limited range of motion. The initial radiographic assessment revealed AVN of the right femoral head, demonstrated by volume loss and deformity of the femoral head, along with acetabular widening. As well, the beginnings of synovial osteochondromatosis were noted, with calcified intra-articular loose bodies identified on imaging (Figure 1). The patient was initially conservatively managed by the orthopedic team.

The solitary (rather than multiple) body is a recognized less-common presentation, so typicality is variant. panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel of excised tissue from a patient with synovial chondromatosis; caption and in-text pathology description support lobular hyaline cartilage, chondrocyte clustering, and ossification characteristic of synovial chondromatosis.

panels.figure_caption: Histological examination of the excised tissue showing that the resected nodules comprise areas of the mature hyaline cartilage surrounded by a thin synovial membrane White arrow showing a cluster of chondrocytes in H and E staining (100x).
in_text_mentions: Vertical capsulotomy of the PIP joint followed by synovectomy was done. After being removed, they were sent for histopathological analysis. Histological studies revealed well-circumcised nodules of osseocartilaginous origin (Figure 4). The cartilage was of moderate cellularity, with varying degrees of ossification, a characteristic feature of synovial chondromatosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial unenhanced thin-slice CT in a published case report of synovial chondromatosis of the hip. The arrowhead marks a homogenous soft tissue-isodense mass filling the right femoroacetabular joint space (non-calcified chondroid synovial mass), with slight acetabular fossa erosion per in-text; real human-patient image clearly attributable to the configured target disease. B: Coronal CT reformat from the same case report of synovial chondromatosis of the hip, displaying the same soft tissue-isodense mass occupying the right femoroacetabular joint space (arrowhead) with joint space widening relative to the contralateral side; a real human-patient image of the target disease, consistent with a non-calcified (variant) presentation.

panels.figure_caption: Un-enhanced thin-slice CT of the hips in transverse-oriented source images (A) and coronal reformats (B). The arrows show the soft tissue-isodense mass, which filled up the right joint space and led to a widening of the joint space compared to the contralateral side. No calcifications or massive extrinsic bone erosions could be seen.
in_text_mentions: An un-enhanced thin-slice CT scan with coronal reformats revealed a slightly widened joint space of the right femoroacetabular joint that was filled with a homogenous soft tissue-isodense material instead of fat and synovial fluid, as seen on the contralateral side (Figure 3). No calcifications could be found within the soft tissue. Slight erosion of the acetabular fossa was evident.

panels.rationale: Single plain radiograph (panel A; the figure as supplied is one radiograph even though the caption also references MRI). The disease-focused article title ('disseminated synovial chondromatosis: a case report') plus the captioned/in-text manifestation support attribution: multiple soft-tissue calcifications within and outside the joint capsule, with the in-text specifying 'multiple intra-articular calcific and ossific loose bodies' and 'large calcified bursal extensions,' matching the calcified intra-articular loose-bodies finding. The plain-film appearance had prompted an impression of idiopathic tumoral calcinosis, but the article diagnosis and prior triage keep the figure under synovial chondromatosis and no caption text names another disease as the panel's diagnosis; it is a real patient image of readable quality and not third-party. The prominent extra-articular calcified masses are proposed because the vocabulary key is intra-articular only. The rare disseminated/extra-articular extent is a recognized less-common (variant) presentation; the caption does not call it atypical. Age/ethnicity are not stated in the provided caption or in-text.

The figure caption explicitly states this is one of the 'two different cases' of MRI loose bodies, and the in-text mention confirms MRI detected loose bodies in 14 patients with synovial chondromatosis in this article about hip SC. Real human-patient diagnostic imaging of a recognized disease manifestation. B: MRI of a second case (open yellow arrow) showing a loose body adjacent to the femoral head in the hip joint space. The caption identifies both sub-images as loose bodies in two cases of synovial chondromatosis, and the in-text context (14 patients with MRI-detected loose bodies in this hip SC cohort) supports disease attribution. Real human-patient diagnostic imaging showing a recognized manifestation of synovial chondromatosis.

in_text_mentions: In two patients (case 1 + 4), repeated biopsy demonstrated benign disease, whilst their imaging studies revealed likely extensive primary synovial chondromatosis. However, it was clear from the patients' level of nonmechanical pain in combination with the rapid and repeated progression of their tumours after debulking that they had aggressive disease. The patients were included in a pragmatic discussion and the decision was made to perform hind-quarter amputation. In both cases, the actual diagnosis of malignancy was only confirmed when the whole tumour had been sampled (see Figures 1 and 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Genuine preoperative T2-weighted shoulder MRI. The disease-focused article title explicitly states subacromial synovial chondromatosis causing a bursal-sided rotator cuff tear, and the panel-specific caption describes a small nearly full-thickness anterior supraspinatus tear. The tear has no allowed vocabulary key, so it is recorded as a proposed finding rather than inferred from general context. b: Real human preoperative MRI showing the diagnostic manifestation of synovial chondromatosis: multiple extratendinous ossific/calcific loose-body densities in the subacromial/subdeltoid bursa. The extratendinous subacromial bursa location is a less common but recognized form, so typicality is variant.

in_text_mentions: houlder were interpreted by a musculoskeletal trained radiologist as calcific densities within the rotator cuff versus extratendinous loose bodies, as well as erosion of the acromioclavicular (AC) joint. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was ordered to accurately assess the exact location of the calcific nodules. MRI (Figure 2) demonstrated multiple extratendinous ossific densities in the subacromial/subdeltoid bursa, consistent with synovial chondromatosis. MRI also demonstrated fraying of the anterior supraspinatus tendon with minimal tendon retraction suggesting a small, full-thickness tear.

panels.rationale: Single coronal STIR MRI of the pelvis in case 4. Disease-focused article title plus the in-text statement that case 4's imaging showed likely extensive primary synovial chondromatosis support attribution to synovial chondromatosis (primary). The image shows a large lobulated hyperintense synovial mass in the right hemipelvis/hip, matching the MRI finding of lobulated synovial chondroid masses; calcific signal voids are not distinctly resolved on this single slice, so no additional finding is asserted. No age/ethnicity stated; no skin shown; only scanner text overlay, no diagnostic annotations. Confidence tempered because the final diagnosis was synovial chondrosarcoma (not a configured target) and only one preoperative slice is shown, but the visible manifestation is consistent with the configured disease. [raw subtype: primary]

in_text_mentions: Plain radiography showed multiple nodules in both the anterior and posterior compartments of the ankle joint. in_text_mentions: otocols can be developed in order to model more adequately such differential diagnosis. Not all clinical settings are able to readily offer the use of MRI in the pursuit of such a rare condition. Also, in our 2 cases who had an MRI exam, FSC was only depicted in one subject, while in the other it was only depicted in the US exam. The use of x-Rays has also been widely utilized in other studies involving SC in the fingers identifying the calcified masses (4–12). Therefore, it may also be possible to standardize the use of x-rays in future studies, as this is a tool easily accessible (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Human patient histopathology from a temporomandibular joint synovial chondromatosis case report. The image and caption show chondrometaplasia of the synovial membrane with mature cartilaginous tissue and endochondral ossification, pathognomonic of synovial chondromatosis; in-text confirms Stage 3 SC of the left TMJ (Milgram). No diagrams, charts, controls, or other diseases. [raw subtype: temporomandibular_joint]

in_text_mentions: Arthrography showed a honeycomb appearance around her left hip joint (Figure 7). Upon MR imaging, axial images of the left hip joint revealed intra-articular and extra-articular mass lesions, one of which was located adjacent to the femoral vessels (Figure 8). These examination findings suggested synovial osteochondromatosis forming a herniation sac. Based on the radiographic features, we considered that arthroscopic resection concomitant with an open anterior approach was suitable for complete resection.

He underwent an X-ray of the right knee, which showed multiple intra-articular and soft tissue calcifications of variable size and shape with relatively preserved joint spaces. Surgical area was irrigated using abundant isotonic solution. The excised mass was sent to pathology laboratory. Pathology evaluation showed that the mass was consistent with synovial chondromatosis (Figure 5). Active and passive exercises were started at an early period after surgery. Recurrence was not detected at his last control visit. Knee movements were at full range when compared with the other knee. There was no pain or other complaints (Figure 6).

panels.figure_caption: CT images from first examination: (a) axial image, (b) coronal image, and (c, d) 3D image. Deformation of the left mandibular condyle is seen, with many small, granular nodules in the area of the left TMJ, some of which are calcified.
in_text_mentions: Panoramic radiography showed that the left mandibular condyle was flattened, with a radiopaque image near the superior joint cavity (Figure 2). The TMJ radiograph also showed deformation in the left mandibular fossa. With mouth opening, both mandibular condyles were able to move to near the lowest point of the articular eminence. CT showed that the left mandibular condyle was flattened, and small and granular nodules were observed in the joint capsule of the left TMJ, some of which were calcified (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Axial CBCT of the left TMJ in a human patient showing a calcified loose body (red arrow), with in-text confirmation of multiple free bodies in the left TMJ space and condylar-neck erosion from compression. The disease-focused title and in-text explicitly attribute this to synovial chondromatosis (fibrous type) of the left TMJ. Calcified intra-articular bodies on CT and pressure cortical scalloping are both supported. [raw subtype: fibrous_type]
panels.attribution_text: Saracutu et al. Synovial chondromatosis of the temporomandibular joint: a case report with an associated systematic review update of the literature.. Journal of oral & facial pain and headache 2025. doi:10.22514/jofph.2025.068. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Axial view of the CBCT. Presence of calcified loose body (red arrow).
in_text_mentions: CT confirmed the presence of at least two of the four free bodies within the left TMJ space (Fig. 3). CT also showed the overall integrity of the condylar cortical structure, with just some signs of erosion of the condylar neck, probably due to the compression caused by the loose bodies. The diagnostic hypothesis of SC of fibrous type of the left TMJ was formulated. panels.rationale: Single-panel sagittal fat-saturated T2-weighted MRI of the left ankle from a case report of bilateral synovial chondromatosis. The image visibly shows two low signal (signal-void) nodules with surrounding effusion posterior to the talo-tibial joint, arrow-annotated, matching calcified chondroid synovial bodies typical of synovial chondromatosis. Prior caption triage confirms real patient radiology, no third-party content. No subtype specified in caption or text, so subtype is null; no ethnicity or age stated; not a skin panel.
panels.attribution_text: Shearer et al. A case report of bilateral synovial chondromatosis of the ankle.. Chiropractic & osteopathy 2007. doi:10.1186/1746-1340-15-18. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Sagittal MRI of the left ankle (fat-saturated T2-weighted) illustrates (arrow) two distinct low signal intensity nodules with surrounding effusion posterior to the talo-tibial joint.
in_text_mentions: discharged from conservative care, the patient was referred for an orthopaedic surgery consult due to the recurrent nature of the ankle pain and the radiographic findings. MR imaging was ordered and revealed calcifications in both ankle joints and the right and left flexor hallucis longus tendon sheaths (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7). Following MR imaging and orthopaedic assessment, the orthopaedic surgeon concluded that surgery to extract the calcifications from the tendons would be too invasive and would not be pursued at the present time. The patient was advised to continue with his daily activities.

panels.rationale: Single-panel AP radiograph of the left hip from a case report titled 'Malignant Transformation of Recurrent Synovial Chondromatosis.' The caption and in-text explicitly describe extensive periarticular soft-tissue calcifications (calcified intra-articular loose bodies) with erosion of the femoral neck (synovial cortical pressure erosion), both classic radiographic manifestations of synovial chondromatosis. The article title is disease-focused on recurrent synovial chondromatosis, supporting disease attribution; the radiographic differential also listed synovial chondrosarcoma, but the underlying disease and the captioned manifestations are those of synovial chondromatosis. Real patient image, clear quality, with white arrows annotating the calcifications. [raw subtype: recurrent]

panels.rationale: Panoramic radiograph of a human patient from a case report titled 'A Case of Synovial Chondromatosis of Temporomandibular Joint with Numerous Loose Bodies.' The caption and in-text explicitly describe flattening of the left mandibular condyle and radiopaque images near the superior joint cavity, corresponding to calcified intra-articular loose bodies and pressure erosion of the condylar cortex—classic radiographic manifestations of synovial chondromatosis of the TMJ.
panels.attribution_text: Matsusue et al. A Case of Synovial Chondromatosis of Temporomandibular Joint with Numerous Loose Bodies.. Case reports in dentistry 2021. doi:10.1155/2021/5927215. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Panoramic radiograph from the first examination. The left mandibular condyle is flattened, and radiopaque images are seen near the superior joint cavity.
in_text_mentions: Panoramic radiography showed that the left mandibular condyle was flattened, with a radiopaque image near the superior joint cavity (Figure 2). The TMJ radiograph also showed deformation in the left mandibular fossa. With mouth opening, both mandibular condyles were able to move to near the lowest point of the articular eminence. CT showed that the left mandibular condyle was flattened, and small and granular nodules were observed in the joint capsule of the left TMJ, some of which were calcified (Figure 3).

B: High-magnification H&E of area I showing clustered chondrocytes within lacunae in a hyaline cartilage matrix, consistent with synovial chondromatosis. Real patient histopathology. C: High-magnification H&E of area II showing cartilage tissue with chondrocytes and areas of fibrosis and ossification, consistent with synovial chondromatosis. Real patient histopathology.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Histopathology from a patient with primary synovial osteochondromatosis of the subdeltoid bursa; caption and in-text describe an early cartilaginous loose body forming within the synovial lining (metaplastic synovial cartilage), a defining feature of synovial chondromatosis. Arrows annotate the findings. b: Histopathology of the same patient showing chondrocytes embedded in newly formed hyaline cartilage, consistent with synovial cartilage metaplasia in primary synovial osteochondromatosis of the subdeltoid bursa, as stated in the article title, caption and in-text. c: Histopathology of the same case showing chondrocytes within lacunae in newly formed cartilage from the cut section of a loose body, a characteristic histologic feature of synovial chondromatosis as described in the caption and in-text.

in_text_mentions: There was no connection of synovial bursa to the joint and all loose bodies remained external to the rotator cuff. A histopathological study revealed the early stages of the development of cartilaginous loose bodies in the synovial lining, suggestive of metaplastic transformation of the synovial tissue [Figure 3a and b]. Areas below the synovial lining contained a large number of mononuclear cells and a fair number of small blood vessels. This was consistent with chronic inflammation. In the cut-section of the loose body, chondrocytes were visible inside the newly formed cartilage [Figure 3c].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal MRI of the pelvis/hips in a human patient; the arrow marks numerous loose bodies in the left hip joint, captioned as suggestive of synovial chondromatosis and confirmed by MRI per the in-text mention. B: Magnified MRI view of the affected hip joint from the same preoperative study, showing the numerous loose bodies captioned as suggestive of synovial chondromatosis. panels.rationale: Single lateral plain radiograph of a human patient's right knee (R marker) demonstrating numerous calcified/ossified nodular bodies clustered within and adjacent to the joint capsule, matching the classic radiographic presentation of synovial chondromatosis. Attribution to synovial chondromatosis rests on the disease-focused article title (bilateral synovial chondromatosis of the knee with intra- and extra-articular disease) together with the specific captioned manifestation (multiple calcifications within and outside the joint capsule). The in-text note that appearances were initially thought consistent with idiopathic tumoral calcinosis slightly lowers confidence, but the case ultimately concerns synovial chondromatosis and no other disease is identified by the caption. The finding corresponds to the vocabulary entry for calcified intra-articular loose bodies; the extra-articular component is listed as a proposed finding. No skin is visible; no age or ethnicity is stated; no staging is described.

panels.body_site: right ankle, flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath
panels.rationale: Single axial proton-density MRI of the right ankle from a case report of bilateral synovial chondromatosis of the ankle. The arrow indicates a heterogeneous nodule of low and intermediate signal in the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath with secondary sheath distension from effusion, directly matching the captioned manifestation of synovial chondromatosis (chondroid synovial mass with calcific low-signal foci). Ankle/tendon-sheath involvement is a recognized less-common presentation, hence variant typicality. No age, ethnicity, or skin assessment is applicable or stated.
panels.attribution_text: Shearer et al. A case report of bilateral synovial chondromatosis of the ankle.. Chiropractic & osteopathy 2007. doi:10.1186/1746-1340-15-18. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Axial MRI of the right ankle (proton density) revealing a (arrow) heterogeneous nodule of low and intermediate signal intensities located in the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath. Of interest is the degree of distension of the tendon sheath secondary to the surrounding effusion.
in_text_mentions: discharged from conservative care, the patient was referred for an orthopaedic surgery consult due to the recurrent nature of the ankle pain and the radiographic findings. MR imaging was ordered and revealed calcifications in both ankle joints and the right and left flexor hallucis longus tendon sheaths (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7). Following MR imaging and orthopaedic assessment, the orthopaedic surgeon concluded that surgery to extract the calcifications from the tendons would be too invasive and would not be pursued at the present time. The patient was advised to continue with his daily activities.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Anteroposterior radiograph of the right knee in a patient with giant synovial chondromatosis, showing a giant irregular calcified intra-articular mass extending from below the patella to the suprapatellar region, consistent with confluent calcified loose bodies. B: Lateral radiograph of the right knee in the same patient, demonstrating the giant irregular calcified mass in the suprapatellar and infrapatellar regions, consistent with calcified intra-articular loose bodies of synovial chondromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: Serbest et al. A neglected case of giant synovial chondromatosis in knee joint.. The Pan African medical journal 2015. doi:10.11604/pamj.2015.22.5.7481. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: X-ray of right knee joint showing the radiodence body. Anteroposterior (a) and lateral (b) X-ray of the knee
in_text_mentions: findings included a solid and semi-mobile mass at anterior knee region. Knee joint range of motion was 80 degrees flexion and 0 degrees extension. There wasn't any neurovascular pathology. Antero-posterior and lateral knee X-rays showed degenerative changes and a giant, irregular, calcific mass which started below patella and extended to suprapatellar area (Figure 1). Knee MRI revealed many loose bodies (consistent with synovial chondromatosis) isointense with fatty bone marrow at all sequences at the level of right knee joint. Scalloping was observed at tibial and femoral surfaces (Figure 2).

panels.body_site: left hand, carpometacarpal joint of the thumb/trapezium and base of first metacarpal
panels.rationale: Single radiograph figure containing PA and lateral projections of the same patient. The disease-focused article title and caption/in-text describe calcified/radiopaque intra-articular bodies around the left thumb carpometacarpal joint, supporting synovial chondromatosis. The hand/thumb CMC location is a less common site, so typicality is variant. No synovial cortical scalloping is tagged because the in-text explicitly states there was no erosion of the first metacarpal base or trapezium.
panels.attribution_text: Yonekura et al. Synovial Osteochondromatosis at the Carpometacarpal Joint of the Thumb.. Case reports in orthopedics 2017. doi:10.1155/2017/3974342. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: PA and lateral plain X-ray of the left hand showing a soft tissue lesion with calcifications adjacent to trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal bone.
in_text_mentions: A plain X-ray of the hand revealed mild soft tissue swelling and radiopaque bodies around the CM joint of the left thumb without erosion of the base of the first metacarpal bone and trapezium (Figure 2). Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed a 2.1 cm × 1.9 cm × 1.4 cm nodule (Figure 3). Due to hospital limitations, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was not obtained.

panels.rationale: Single coronal arthro-CT image of the pelvis in a human patient from a case report of massive synovial osteochondromatosis of the hip. The caption and in-text explicitly attribute the lesion to synovial osteochondromatosis (honeycomb appearance, herniation sac), and the image visibly shows extensive calcified chondral bodies within/around the left hip joint with an extra-articular herniation sac (arrowhead). The right hip serves as a normal comparison within the same clinical scan, which is acceptable as a real patient image. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text, and no staging is given.
panels.attribution_text: Kataoka et al. Complete Resection of a Massive Synovial Osteochondromatosis of the Hip Using an Anterior Approach: A Report of Two Cases.. Case reports in orthopedics 2017. doi:10.1155/2017/9806863. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Arthro-computerised tomography scan of the left hip joint. The extra-articular herniation sac is indicated by the arrowhead.

Arthrography and computed tomography (CT) images of the left hip joint also revealed a honeycomb appearance of the lesion (Figure 3). These examination findings suggested that the tumour was a synovial osteochondromatosis forming a herniation sac. panels.rationale: Real patient anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis/hip from a case report of massive synovial osteochondromatosis of the hip. The captioned manifestation (enlargement of the acetabular fossa, marked by the black arrow) reflects pressure erosion/remodeling of adjacent bone cortex caused by the intra-articular disease, matching the cortical scalloping finding. The caption emphasizes this pressure-erosion change rather than the hallmark multiple calcified loose bodies, so it is treated as a recognized variant presentation. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings are stated, and it is not an AS case.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient PA radiograph of the right thumb from a case report of tenosynovial chondromatosis of the flexor pollicis longus tendon (a subtype of primary synovial chondromatosis). The caption attributes the dorsolateral soft tissue swelling to the lesion; notably there is no bony scalloping/erosion and no calcified loose bodies, so no vocabulary finding key applies and the visible swelling is listed as proposed. in_text_mentions: of her left shoulder and proximal part of her left arm which she had first noticed 2 years ago. The swelling was obstructing the movements of her affected shoulder and was cosmetically unacceptable [Figure 1a]. She had no history of trauma or fever. Her appetite was not affected, and there had been no weight loss. The globular swelling was painless and measured approximately 8 inches in diameter. No tenderness or warmth, but some pseudofluctuation was observed, along with restriction of all movements except adduction. No abnormality was detected in central nervous, cardiovascular, respiratory

On MRI, multiple nonosseous loose bodies were visualized in the bursa deep to the deltoid muscle. These spread up to the subacromial space as well as the anterior and posterior aspects of the shoulder. These appeared to remain outside the rotator cuff [Figure 1c and d]. Aspiration returned the nonhemorrhagic synovial fluid with no sign of tuberculosis or other chronic infective pathology.

panels.rationale: Single-panel panoramic radiograph from a human patient in an article titled 'Surgical treatment of a rare bilateral synovial chondromatosis.' Caption and in-text explicitly state radiopaque loose bodies in both TMJs, and the in-text notes the diagnostic hypothesis of bilateral synovial chondromatosis (SC) was raised. Arrows annotate the loose bodies. This is a real patient image showing the classic calcified intra-articular loose bodies of synovial chondromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: Barretto et al. Surgical treatment of a rare bilateral synovial chondromatosis.. Autopsy & case reports 2020. doi:10.4322/acr.2020.183. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Panoramic X-ray showing Loose bodies on the right and left side of TMJ (arrows).
in_text_mentions: MJ, and intense bilateral articular pain. Some teeth were absent, there was occlusal contact only at anterior teeth, and the median line was aligned (Figure 1B). TMJ radiography revealed radiopaque images in both TMJs (Figure 2). The CT confirmed the presence of loose bodies in TMJ bilaterally. Those bodies measured approximately 13 mm in the left, and 8mm in the right side (Figure 3A and 3B). There was a reduction of TMJ space associated with sclerosis. Due to the slow evolution process associated with clinical and imaging characteristics, the diagnostic hypothesis of bilateral SC was raised.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real human-patient preoperative sagittal T1WI MRI of the right TMJ in a confirmed synovial chondromatosis case (article title and prior triage). The image shows a mass expanding the joint space with multiple loose bodies, a classic MRI presentation of lobulated synovial chondroid masses in synovial chondromatosis. Red arrow annotation present; no third-party issue. Age/ethnicity not stated. B: Real human-patient preoperative coronal PDWI MRI of the right TMJ in the same synovial chondromatosis case. A heterogeneous signal-intensity tissue mass within the joint capsule between the glenoid fossa and mandibular condyle corresponds to lobulated cartilaginous synovial masses of synovial chondromatosis. Red arrow annotation present; disease attribution supported by caption and disease-focused title. Age/ethnicity not stated.

panels.rationale: Axial fat-suppressed PD MRI of the wrist shows a volar DRUJ synovial capsular proliferation/thickened capsule, compatible with the article's diagnosis of synovial chondromatosis. The finding is centered on the target disease, though the capsular proliferation is not fully specific and calcified bodies are explicitly absent.
panels.attribution_text: Mert et al. Synovial chondromatosis of the distal radioulnar joint-a rare case.. Journal of surgical case reports 2024. doi:10.1093/jscr/rjae394. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial slice of a fat suppressed PD Dixon—synovial capsular proliferation on the volar aspect of the DRUJ (asterix); the capsule is thickened, additionally evidence of hypointense internal structures aside the capsular proliferation.
in_text_mentions: MRI scan revealed suspicion of ganglion cyst formation. The images (Figs 1 and 2) depicted a palmar-directed mass originating from the DRUJ with a transverse diameter measuring a maximum of 12 x 17 mm. The mass exhibited a predominant fluid isointense internal signal, accompanied by marginal signal depressions on T2-weighted sequence. These depressions within the suspected ganglion raised suspicion of diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor. The mass had contact to the flexor tendons at the level of the DRUJ. No pathological bone marrow edema was observed.

Our case presented an intra-articular SC with direct infiltration of the DRUJ, where preoperative MRI scans (Figs 1 and 2) did not reveal evidence of calcified bodies, bone bruise, or periosteal reaction. Therefore, the accurate diagnosis was suspected intraoperatively and confirmed by histopathological examination. Similar discoveries during surgery were documented by Misawa et al. and Rogachefsky et al. in the literature [3, 4]. Kim et al. reported in 2015 that no free chondral bodies were found in the surrounding tissue of their case [5].

in_text_mentions: th a diameter of about 0.5 to 2.0 cm. The chondroid granules in the capsule were cleaned completely, the wall of the capsule was separated from the surrounding tissues, and the capsule was excised completely and sent for pathological examination. The incision was closed. Intraoperative blood loss was approximately 900 mL, thus we used erythrocyte 2U. The postoperative pathology confirmed the diagnosis of synovial osteochondromatosis of the thigh (Fig. 5A–F). Pathological result was positive for Vimentin and S-100. Biopsy samples were negative for AE1/AE3 and EMA, with 5% Ki-67 positive nuclei.
